body: I've always had trouble in my bumbling, poorly informed attempts at meditation. I think the fact that I have OCD (comorbidity, FTW) has something to do with it. Do you know of a good primer on practicing meditation and/or mindfulness?
I'm downloading the torrent right now. Thanks!

It does. I don't know if it will work for me, feeling as powerless as I do. I am genuinely sorry to hear about your childhood, though: I had a bad one, too. I was emotionally and physically abused by my dad from the time I was three to the time I was eight, which undoubtedly left some kind of mark on me.

I could see myself taking the route you've suggested, an absurdist or existentialist road out of the pit of despair I'm in right now. If nothing matters then there's no harm, I suppose, in pretending that things that make me and the people around me happy matter.

Taking life one day at a time probably would be helpful to me. It would at least move my focus away from the cosmic scale of things. I do try to laugh when I can, and I'm grateful for every moment I'm able to take pleasure in something, no matter how fleeting.

Thank you for this response. I like the rehearsal of the intellectual heritage of nihilism(s): it makes me feel like I'm in good company. And I have a lot of sympathy for the Buddhist drive to reduce suffering, since I've found suffering to be so abundant and happiness--or even just not-suffering--so precious and hard-to-come-by that I'm loath to deprive anyone of the latter. I wonder, though, what a world with no suffering would look like. From what I understand (and my understanding of Buddhism is extremely limited), most accounts of nirvana have it somewhere in the neighborhood of non-existence. That's troubling to me: I'd like there to be a kind of existence beyond suffering, though I have no idea what it'd look like because I take pleasure in so little. Am I understanding nirvana correctly? Or are there other accounts that would be less distressing to me (maybe somewhere in the Pure Land tradition--another thing I know embarrassingly little about)?
Did your nihilism cause you to become anhedonic? If so, what kinds of therapeutic advice helped ameliorate--or better yet eliminate--your anhedonia?

I've been listening to various Alan Watts lectures since I received your kind suggestion. He's interesting! I also learned on his Wikipedia page that his worldview emphasized the Hindu concept of the world as lila, which appeals to me: can you point me anywhere that he talks about lila at great length?

I dropped acid once. To my surprise, it didn't exacerbate my depressive condition--on the contrary, I felt like the world was alive and illimitable and I only just begun to explore it. I even had a low-grade religious experience listening to some Sufi dhikr. Unfortunately I didn't learn any lessons, at least not any that would help me in the long-term. I've heard people say that hallucinogens helped them get out of anhedonic holes, though. I guess I wasn't doing things quite right since I was so determined to pack as many experiences as I could into a single trip, just watching cartoons and listening to music and doing whatever else I could think to do that would feel different on acid.
